beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about in-context learning, when a model picks up a pattern from examples in its own prompt, with no weight updates at all, and three questions that test what that actually can and can't do.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01.

beats.narration_text: Show a model a handful of examples right in its prompt, and it'll often complete a brand new case perfectly. That looks exactly like learning something new. But nothing gets written to a single weight. Whatever it picked up has to already be reachable from what's in that prompt and whatever it already knew going in. Sometimes that's enough. Sometimes it only looks like enough.
beats.new_visual_element: A prompt window with a few example pairs, a new query resolving to a correct answer, then an overlay posing the real question: is this learning, or is this locating?

shot.note: Generic/hypothetical scenario -- no real model named, per FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: Here's the test, before any example: three questions. One, spot the mapping: can you tell, just from the examples, what pattern they're pointing the model toward? Two, shuffle the set: reorder the examples, change how many there are, or swap which ones you pick, does the answer survive? If it flips, that's fragile pattern-matching, not a stable rule. Three, push past the window: does the task need more than fits in the prompt, or a capability the model never had to begin with? If so, no number of examples will produce it. If the pattern only holds for one ordering, one count, or something already latent, that's the boundary, not a bug.
beats.new_visual_element: Checklist card, all 3 tests shown together (Spot the Mapping / Shuffle the Set / Push Past the Window)

shot.note: Framework shown fully before any example, matching prior STEM videos' rubric beat.

beats.narration_text: Here's how it actually works. Put a made-up rule entirely inside the prompt: a handful of examples, each one an input and the output that rule produces, no explanation given. Then hand it a brand new input the rule was never shown directly. A model can often produce the right output anyway, not because it learned a new capability, but because it located a pattern its own architecture is already built to complete, using nothing but what's sitting in the context window right now.
beats.new_visual_element: 4 example pairs stacking into a prompt panel, a new input arriving, the correct output resolving, tagged LOCATED, NOT LEARNED

shot.note: [Source: FACTCHECK.md #2/#3 -- generic illustration of a documented pattern, no real model named] The rule, the new input, and the output must all be visible together so the mechanism reads without narration alone.

beats.narration_text: Now the case that would break this test if it were sloppy. Take the exact same style of task. Reorder the same examples, and flip just one of the mappings so it goes against what the model's own training would expect. Ask the identical new question. This time the output gets inconsistent, or quietly reverts to the more familiar pattern instead of the one actually demonstrated. Same task shape, same number of examples, a completely different, and much less reliable, result.
beats.new_visual_element: The same example-panel layout, reordered, one mapping visibly flipped, the output tagged MISMATCH instead of a clean resolution

shot.note: Stress-tests the framework against a naive 'a few examples always teach the model the rule' over-trigger. Visually distinct resolution from B04 (mismatch tag vs clean resolution).

beats.narration_text: Here's something to try today, on any system you have access to. Invent a small rule with no real-world meaning, so you know any correct answer has to come from the prompt itself. Give it four or five examples, then test it on new inputs it hasn't seen. Now shuffle the same examples and test the same inputs again. Then flip one example's mapping and test once more. If the answers only hold for the original order, you've just found the edge of what that prompt can actually teach.
beats.new_visual_element: The 3 tests restated as a checklist card

shot.note: Concrete action, not a restatement of B03 -- should read as a checklist/task card, not another copy of the framework card.

beats.narration_text: In-context learning is powerful pattern-location, not instant new learning. It's bounded by what the model already had latent going in, and by what actually fits, in a stable way, inside the prompt.
